newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope says committed to unity, Orthodox stay away.
newsitem.headline: Pope says committed to unity, Orthodox stay away.

text.p: Pope John Paul renewed his commitment to the goal of Christian unity on Sunday as representatives of the Orthodox Church boycotted his solemn mass on an important feast day.
The service was held to mark the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, who brought Christianity to Rome and were both martyred there during Roman persecutions.

It is one of the most important days of the Roman Catholic church's liturgical calendar and a symbol of the quest for unity between the Western and Eastern Christian churches because the apostles lived a millennium before the split in 1054.
The congregation of some 10,000 people in St Peter's Basilica prayed for Christian unity during the service.
"I feel committed to being an ardent promoter of this unity," the 77-year-old Pontiff told pilgrims and tourists in St Peter's Square after the mass.

The Vatican announced last week that for the first time in 21 years, the Orthodox Church was not sending a delegation to the annual feast to represent the Ecumenical Patriarch of Istanbul, Bartholomew.
Two weeks ago, the Russian Orthodox church pulled out of a proposed historic meeting in Vienna between its Patriarch Alexiy and the Polish Pope.
Orthodox churches have voiced sharp criticism at a European Ecumenical Conference in Graz, Austria, which was ending on Sunday, about the missionary work of the Catholic church in Eastern Europe.

If Patriarch Alexiy and the Pope had met, it would have been the first encounter of its kind since the schism which split western Christian churches looking to Rome and the eastern church based in Constantinople -- now Istanbul.
During the mass, the Pope gave a liturgical vestment known as the pallium to 29 Catholic archbishops who were appointed during the last year.

The pallium is a circular band of white wool that is marked with six crosses and worn around the neck. It is a symbol of the episcopal office and of the unity between the bishops and the Pope in Rome.

Among the new archbishops who received the pallium from the Pope were George Pell of Melbourne, Australia, Sean Brady of Armagh, Ireland, Ivan Dias of Bombay, India, Charles Chaput of Denver, Francis George of Chicago, and Emmanuel Kataliko of Bukavu, Congo and Simon Ntamwana of Gitega, Burundi.
Mother Teresa of Calcutta attended the mass. At the end of the service she was brought to the Pope in a wheelchair and rose to her feet to embrace him and kiss his hand.
The 86-year-old Noble Peace Prize winner has just arrived in Rome from New York and is expected to return to her home in India soon.
Mother Teresa stepped down as head of the Missionaries of Charity order in March after a battle against heart disease.

The Pope, who has suffered from a series of health problems in recent years, appeared in good form during the two-and-a-half hour service although he had to wipe sweat from his forehead in the stifiling Rome heat.
